Use global Gibbs-energy support to assess candidate liquid phases.

## Phase equilibrium includes stability

Equality of chemical potentials identifies stationary candidate states. Stable equilibrium requires the lowest admissible total Gibbs energy.

$$g_{mix}/RT=\sum_i x_i\ln x_i+g^E/(RT)$$

A split can lower G even when a homogeneous liquid is locally stable.

::: {.notes}
Review ideal mixing plus excess Gibbs. Distinguish Gibbs energy per mole from total Gibbs when applying the lever rule.
:::

## Binodal and spinodal

![Module 5 reference illustration: coexistence and local instability are different boundaries.](figures/f5_01_gmix_binodal_spinodal.png){width="78%"}

::: {.notes}
Point out metastable regions between binodal and spinodal. Ask where a second derivative test is insufficient.
:::

## The common-tangent conditions

$$g'(x^\alpha)=g'(x^\beta)=\frac{g(x^\beta)-g(x^\alpha)}{x^\beta-x^\alpha}$$

The tangent must not lie above g(x) anywhere in the admitted composition interval.

A trivial root xᵅ=xᵝ does not establish two distinct liquid phases.

::: {.notes}
Derive the chemical-potential intercept interpretation. Numerical equality plus distinct compositions still needs global support.
:::

## Tangent-plane distance

For a trial composition w relative to reference z,
$$TPD(w;z)=g(w)-g(z)-g'(z)(w-z)$$

A negative value identifies a Gibbs-energy-lowering perturbation. Local curvature examines only the neighborhood of z.

Lab 04 evaluates the binary model; it is not a general multicomponent TPD package.

::: {.notes}
Use consistent dimensionless g/RT if demonstrating the plotted TPD. TPD of a candidate multiphase support line differs from this one-reference expression but shares the supporting-plane principle.
:::

## A lever-rule calculation

Synthetic tie line: x₁ᵅ=0.2, x₁ᵝ=0.8. Feed z₁=0.5.

$$f_\beta=\frac{z_1-x_1^\alpha}{x_1^\beta-x_1^\alpha}=0.5$$

For z₁=0.35, fᵝ=0.25. At the same coexistence conditions, the phase amounts change but the tie-line endpoints do not.

::: {.notes}
Treat the tie line as a given hypothetical calculation, not a claimed output of the default parameter set. Check both component and total balances.
:::

## Model shape and liquid splitting

Positive activity deviations alone do not guarantee LLE. The mixing Gibbs-energy shape must support a split.

The labs include Margules and NRTL options with different shapes. Standard Wilson behavior is discussed in the reference deck, not implemented as an LLE solver here.

::: {.notes}
Avoid conflating number of parameters with ability to split. Ask students to identify where ideal mixing competes with excess Gibbs.
:::

## LLE fitting uses different evidence

Tie-line data constrain the coexistence compositions. Fitting must reproduce distinct phases and a supported common tangent.

A small tie-line error at one T does not establish a unique parameter set or a temperature law.

Lab 05 retains the input observations and checks stability of the fitted result.

::: {.notes}
Discuss parameter identifiability and why fixing alpha matters. Repeated measurements are evidence, not duplicate points to silently discard.
:::

## Guided exploration · 35 minutes

Choose one state with a supported liquid split.

Predict the effect of changing z while holding T and model fixed. Record phase compositions and amounts, then check the lever rule.

Use a fitting example to state one parameter uncertainty that a small residual cannot resolve.

::: {.notes}
Require distinct compositions and a reported global check. Students may compare two near-equivalent fits but must label that exploration, not a formal confidence interval.
:::

## Vapor–liquid–liquid coexistence

$$\hat f_i^V=\hat f_i^{L\alpha}=\hat f_i^{L\beta}$$

For a binary nonreacting system with three phases, the phase rule gives one intensive degree of freedom before imposing T or P.

Phase compositions and phase amounts are different unknowns. Specifying T and P does not always uniquely determine all amounts.

::: {.notes}
Use the conventional F=C−P+2 with C=2 and P=3; the symbol P here means phase count, not pressure. Say this verbally to avoid notation ambiguity.
:::

## Three phase amounts can form a family

Given three fixed binary phase compositions,
$$f_\alpha+f_\beta+f_V=1$$
$$z_1=f_\alpha x_1^\alpha+f_\beta x_1^\beta+f_Vy_1$$

There are two independent constraints on three fractions. Nonnegativity bounds the feasible family. Another independent extensive constraint may select a member.

::: {.notes}
This is the pedagogical reason Lab 06 exposes feasible fractions rather than fabricating a unique answer.
:::

## VLLE extension

[Open Lab 06](labs/vlle.html#vl-experiment)

Compare the supported liquid and vapor states. Move within the admissible phase-fraction family and verify the overall balance.

Identify a state where the vapor fraction is constrained by nonnegativity. Explain why equal fugacities alone cannot determine every fraction.

::: {.notes}
Optional independent work. Do not require completion during the already allocated core fitting exercise.
:::

## Where the model can be reused

A fitted liquid model needs a matching component order, parameter convention and temperature before reuse.

VLE also requires pure-component vapor pressures and a vapor model. LLE experimental pressure is not a vapor-pressure correlation.

A new phase calculation brings new assumptions and validation needs.

::: {.notes}
This addresses the Lab 05 to Lab 01 transfer: explicitly supply matching saturation pressures; no automatic invention.
:::

## Exit question

A solver reports two liquid compositions with equal chemical potentials and a tiny residual.

What checks distinguish a real stable split from a trivial or metastable result?

Which quantities change when only the overall composition changes?

::: {.notes}
Expected: distinct phases, nonnegative amounts, global supporting tangent, balance; phase fractions change along a fixed tie line.
:::

## Independent practice · suggested 60–90 minutes

A common-tangent result, one lever-rule check and one limitation of the fitted parameters.

Retain the calculator export, your worksheet, a comparison plot/table and one independent check. State an assumption that limits your conclusion.

Use the core labs on the [learning path](labs/learning-path.html#session-3). Optional extensions are additional work.
